4.text: At last the light is put out and the shaman begins to operate. He

5.text: beats the drum and sings his introductory tunes, at first in a low voice; then

6.text: gradually his voice increases in volume, and soon it fills the small closed-up

7.text: room with its violent clamor. The narrow walls resound in all directions.

8.text: Moreover, the shaman uses his drum for modifying his voice, now placing

9.text: it directly before his mouth, now turning it at an oblique angle, and all the

10.text: time beating it violently. After a few minutes, all this noise begins to work

11.text: strangely on the listeners, who are crouching down, squeezed together in a

12.text: most uncomfortable position. They begin to lose the power to locate the

13.text: source of the sounds; and, almost without any effort of imagination, the song

14.text: and the drum seem to shift from corner to corner, or even to move about

15.text: without having any definite place at all.

16.text: The shaman’s songs have no words. Their music is mostly simple, and

17.text: consists of one short phrase repeated again and again. After repeating it

18.text: many times, the shaman breaks off, and utters a series of long-drawn,

19.text: hysterical sighs, which sound something like “Ah, ya, ka, ya, ka, ya, ka!”

20.text: After that, he comes back to his songs. For this he draws his breath as

23.text: Some of the tunes, however, are more varied, and are not devoid of a

24.text: certain grace. Not a few are improvised by the shaman on the spot; others

25.text: are repeated from seance to seance. Each shaman has several songs of his

26.text: own, which are well known to the people; so that if anybody uses one of

27.text: them, for instance at a ceremonial, the listeners recognize it immediately, and

30.text: There is no definite order for the succession of the songs, and the shaman

31.text: changes them at will, sometimes even returning to the first one after a con-

32.text: siderable interval has elapsed. This introductory singing lasts from a quarter of

33.text: an hour to half an hour or more, after which the keˊlet make their first appearance.

34.text: The shaman sings all alone, and the auditors take no part in the perform-

35.text: ance. From time to time, however, some one of the listeners will cry out,

36.text: “Hɪk, hɪk!” or “Hɪč, hɪč!” (interjection of wonder) or “Qaiˊvo” (“of course”)

37.text: or “Emñoˊlɪk” (“certainly”), — all of which are meant to express the full

38.text: approbation by those present of the doings of the shaman. The Chukchee

39.text: have a special word for these exclamations, — oˊčɪtkɵk (“to give answering

40.text: calls”). Without an očɪtkɵˊlɪn (participle), a Chukchee shaman considers

41.text: himself unable to perform his calling in a proper way; therefore novices, while

42.text: trying to learn the shamanistic practices, unsually induce a brother or a sister
